reason: Chest pain and emergency treatment during transport are listed presumptive conditions, and the beneficiary had been discharged earlier that day from a residence origin, so the inpatient rule does not displace Part B.
Multiple therapy disciplines, near-daily PT/OT, daily physician contact and measurable functional gains support coverage; the 3-hour measure is not the only way to show intensity.
Nurse administration of oral meds is not skilled when a caregiver gives them, skilled observation ended with stability, and physician signature/plan-of-care documentation is doubtful.
Prothrombin monitoring was reasonable because the Coumadin dose was being adjusted, with INR above safe range, and the plan of care specified service type and frequency.
The patient was stable with normal vitals, no treatment, and no emergency or presumptive condition, so medical necessity for BLS emergency transport is not shown.
Air transport requires that ground ambulance be inappropriate; the appellant conceded ground transport to a closer hospital was reasonable and the patient was stable.
Hospital-to-hospital transport is covered only if the sending hospital lacked adequate facilities; the record identifies no missing service and the sending hospital also had a trauma center.
The cardiologist stated monitored ambulance transport was necessary after recent pacemaker surgery and oxygen was required, supporting necessity despite the patient's ability to walk.
Daily PT and OT met the multiple-discipline requirement and measurable practical improvement was expected and achieved.
The inpatient decision was reverted to observation and the discharge summary describes observation, so inpatient admission requirements are not met.
The destination was a physician-staffed urgent care clinic, and ambulance service to a physician-directed clinic is not covered.

Infrequent absences including adult day care do not defeat homebound status, taxing effort to leave home was documented, and unstable blood sugars with medication changes justified skilled observation.
The beneficiary was formally admitted to inpatient status after observation and the stay spanned two midnights, with no contrary finding on necessity.
The transfer was supported by cardiac distress and lack of a cardiologist, but payment is limited to the distance to the nearer appropriate hospital (133 of 203 miles).
Physician-ordered dysphagia therapy by an SLP was skilled, needed due to injury, and produced documented gains; coverage does not depend solely on improvement potential.
Skilled observation was not justified: longstanding pattern, no medication or plan changes, no documented teaching, and no documented rationale for potential complication.
No physician statement of homebound status and regular outings four days a week without established day-care licensure fail the qualifying criteria.
Filling a mediplanner and overseeing aides is not skilled care, no observation orders or changes in condition, and aide hours exceeded the part-time limit.
No passage bars the stay; the record documents surgical extent and pulmonary status as reasons for hospitalization and nothing shows a non-covered related service.
Nurses documented assessment, wound care and caregiver teaching for pressure ulcer and skin wounds, which is skilled care regardless of stage.
Diabetes was controlled orally with normal readings, family handled medications, and the plan of care was signed late with the nurse signature missing.
Skilled gait training was documented each visit under a physician order specifying type and frequency, with fall-risk score improving materially.
